title: Three simple values
materials: desk lamp or another steady lamp
objective: Group a lit fruit and its cast shadow into light, middle, and dark values while keeping the chosen crop readable.

warmup.instructions: Place one fruit under a steady lamp. Make a palm-sized thumbnail with three broad pencil values: light, middle, and dark. Keep the silhouette and cast shadow simple; do not blend. Squint once to check whether the three groups stay distinct.

explanation: Value means how light or dark an area looks. Squint at the fruit to simplify small changes into broad light, middle, and dark groups. Keep these groups distinct before adding small details.
A form shadow turns across the fruit. A cast shadow falls from the fruit onto the table, away from the lamp. Observe both shapes and keep the cast shadow connected to the fruit's base.

exercise.instructions:
1. (4 min) Set one fruit under a steady lamp. Choose your viewpoint and crop so the fruit and its full cast shadow fit on the page.
2. (5 min) Compare the fruit's height and width. Lightly place its outline, stem if visible, and the shadow's direction and outer edge.
3. (7 min) Squint at the subject. Mark the broad light area, the turning middle, and the darker form and cast shadows. Keep the cast shadow as one connected shape.
4. (11 min) Shade with broad, even marks. Leave the light group mostly as paper; use a middle value for the turning plane and a darker value for the shadows. Let the observed fruit decide each boundary.
5. (4 min) Squint again and compare the page with life. Correct one unclear boundary or value group; stop before texture and tiny highlights.

bookReferences.note: Printed folios in the supplied scan. Pages 104 and 110 inform observing light and shadow as the lamp changes; p. 117 addresses cast-shadow drawing. The light/middle/dark key is a course simplification, not a prescribed three-step scale in the source.
Simplified value masses in thumbnails inform the small composition/value check; the fruit-and-shadow exercise and three-group key remain original course directions.

reflection: Can you still distinguish light, middle, and dark when you squint at your drawing?
Does the cast shadow point away from the lamp as it does in the setup?
Does your crop keep the fruit and its shadow together as one clear arrangement?
extension: Move the lamp slightly and make a three-minute thumbnail. Note which cast-shadow edge or value boundary changed.

teaching.whyItMatters: Grouping values makes the fruit turn in space while keeping its shape readable before surface detail takes over.
teaching.connections: Lesson 6 asked you to choose a clear crop and inspect its surrounding gaps. Carry that frame forward so the fruit and full cast shadow remain one readable arrangement; use the light, middle, and dark groups to clarify form.

deepDive: A value is how light or dark a shape appears. When you squint, small shifts in brightness soften and larger areas become easier to compare. For this exercise, simplify what you see into three families: light, middle, and dark. This is a temporary beginner's key, not a rule that every object has exactly three values. A lit area may be gray rather than white, and a shadow may contain quieter changes that you can leave for later.

Keep the fruit's form shadow separate in your thinking from its cast shadow. The form shadow follows the turning surface; the cast shadow lies on the table and changes shape with the lamp's direction and distance. Dodson's lamp comparisons and cast-shadow study support looking for those relationships, while the broad three-group key here is our own simplification. After grouping, compare the shadow edges and fruit silhouette with the real setup, just as you compared shapes and gaps while choosing a crop in Lesson 6. Picard's thumbnail section on printed pp. 81–82 uses simplified value masses to compare small compositions. Test the fruit and its cast shadow together at thumbnail scale before committing; then carry the same readable frame into the larger drawing and refine only the value boundaries your observation supports. At the edges between adjacent masses, keep the boundary where the light actually changes; squinting simplifies the pattern but should not erase a sharp contact edge or blend separate shadows.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding many small patches before the large value groups read clearly.
commonMistakes.lookFor: When you squint, the fruit's light, middle, and dark areas break apart, and the cast shadow stops reading as one shape.

Does the cast shadow sit on the table and extend away from the lamp?
Does the selected crop include the full shadow without an accidental near-touch at the page edge?
